title: CELPIP Reading: The Four Parts
summary: CELPIP Reading's four real-life parts — correspondence, a diagram, information and viewpoints — and how to work them fast.

nodes.label: Reading Correspondence
nodes.note: A letter/email + a reply to complete

nodes.label: Apply a Diagram
nodes.note: Match a diagram to a message

chunks.heading: Reading Correspondence — a message and a reply
chunks.body: You read a **letter or email**, then complete a **related reply** by choosing the words that fit. It tests whether you follow the message's **details and tone**. Read the original carefully — the reply's blanks depend on facts and feelings in it.
chunks.realExample: If the email complains about a late delivery, the reply's blanks will hinge on that complaint — pick options that match the situation and an appropriate, polite tone.
chunks.memoryHook: Read the message for facts + tone; the reply's blanks come straight from it.

chunks.heading: Reading to Apply a Diagram
chunks.body: You're given a **diagram or a set of options plus a message**, and you **match information between them** — for example, picking the right choice from a table based on what an email says. It's practical, everyday reading, not academic.
chunks.realExample: A message describes what someone needs (a size, a date, a budget); you scan a chart and choose the option that fits all their conditions.
chunks.memoryHook: Match the message's requirements to the diagram. Find the option that fits all conditions.

chunks.heading: Reading for Information — match to paragraphs
chunks.body: You read a **longer informational passage** split into paragraphs and answer questions that **map to specific paragraphs**. Skim for structure first, then locate the paragraph each question points to — don't reread the whole thing per question.
chunks.realExample: If a question asks about a specific fact, find the paragraph that covers that topic and read only there — the passage's structure tells you where to look.
chunks.memoryHook: Skim the structure, then jump to the right paragraph. Don't reread everything.

chunks.heading: Reading for Viewpoints — opinions and attitude
chunks.body: You read an **article expressing opinions** (often with comments), and answer questions about **who thinks what** and each person's **attitude**. Track the different viewpoints — the trap is mixing up whose opinion is whose.
chunks.realExample: If the writer supports a policy but a commenter opposes it, a question may ask the commenter's view — keep the viewpoints clearly separated as you read.
chunks.memoryHook: Separate the viewpoints — who supports, who opposes, and the attitude of each.

recall.q: What do you do in the 'Reading Correspondence' part?
recall.a: Read a letter or email, then complete a related reply by choosing the words that fit its details and tone.

recall.q: What does 'Reading to Apply a Diagram' involve?
recall.a: Matching information between a message and a diagram or set of options — practical, everyday reading.

recall.q: How should you approach 'Reading for Information'?
recall.a: Skim the passage's structure, then jump to the specific paragraph each question maps to, rather than rereading everything.

recall.q: What is the key skill in 'Reading for Viewpoints'?
recall.a: Tracking the different opinions and attitudes — keeping clear who thinks what.

recall.q: Is there a penalty for wrong answers in CELPIP Reading?
recall.a: No — multiple-choice items have no penalty, so always answer every question.
